title: Density
aim: To determine the densities of regularly shaped objects, irregularly shaped objects and liquids by measuring their mass and volume.
background: Density is the mass per unit volume of a material. It is calculated using density = mass ÷ volume (ρ = m ÷ V). In SI units density is measured in kg/m³, but in the laboratory it is often easier to measure mass in grams and volume in cm³, giving density in g/cm³. To convert from g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000.

Mass is measured with a top pan balance. For a regularly shaped object, such as a cuboid, the volume is calculated from its measured dimensions: volume = length × width × height. A ruler can be used for large objects, but vernier callipers or a micrometer give better resolution for small objects.

For an irregularly shaped object, the volume is found by displacement. A eureka (displacement) can is filled with water until it overflows from the spout. When the object is lowered in, it pushes out a volume of water equal to its own volume, which is collected in a measuring cylinder. Alternatively, the object can be lowered into a measuring cylinder of water and the rise in water level read.

For a liquid, an empty measuring cylinder is placed on a balance and the balance is set to zero (tared). A known volume of liquid is poured in and its mass is read directly. Density depends on the particle arrangement: solids and liquids have much higher densities than gases because their particles are close together.
hypothesis: Objects made of the same material will have the same density whatever their shape or size, and metals will have higher densities than stone, water or oil.

variables.independent: Material of the object or liquid being tested.
variables.dependent: Density (g/cm³), calculated from the measured mass and volume.
control: Same top pan balance, checked to read zero before each measurement
Same measuring cylinder, read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
Eureka can filled to the level of the spout before each object is added

equipment: 10 cm³ measuring cylinder for small volumes
Regularly shaped objects (aluminium cube, steel cuboid)
method: Regular object: measure the mass of the object on a top pan balance and record it in grams.
Measure the length, width and height of the object with a ruler or vernier callipers. Measure each dimension in a few places and calculate a mean.
Calculate the volume using volume = length × width × height, then calculate density = mass ÷ volume.
Irregular object: measure the mass of the object on the balance.
Place the eureka can on the bench and fill it with water until water runs out of the spout. Wait until it stops dripping.
Place an empty measuring cylinder under the spout.
Tie the object to a piece of thread and lower it slowly into the eureka can until it is completely under the water. Do not drop it, as this splashes water out.
When the water stops dripping, read the volume of water in the measuring cylinder at eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus. This equals the volume of the object. Calculate its density.
Liquid: place an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and set the balance to zero.
Pour 50.0 cm³ of the liquid into the measuring cylinder, reading the volume at eye level. Record the mass shown on the balance.
Calculate the density of the liquid using density = mass ÷ volume.
Repeat each measurement three times and calculate a mean density for each material. Convert to kg/m³ by multiplying by 1000 if needed.

safety.hazard: Spilled water or oil on the floor
safety.precaution: Stand the eureka can in a tray, wipe up spills straight away with paper towels.

safety.risk: Injury if dropped on feet or hands.
safety.precaution: Keep blocks away from the edge of the bench and handle them carefully.

safety.hazard: Water near the electric top pan balance
safety.risk: Electric shock or damage to the balance.
safety.precaution: Keep the eureka can away from the balance and dry objects before weighing them.

results.notes: Density = mass ÷ volume. Volumes of regular objects were calculated from their dimensions. The volume of the stone is the volume of water it displaced from the eureka can. Liquid masses were read directly from the balance after taring the empty measuring cylinder (for the oil, the empty cylinder had a mass of 62.5 g and the cylinder plus oil 108.3 g, giving 45.8 g). Results are given to 3 significant figures (2 for oil). To convert to kg/m³, multiply by 1000: aluminium 2700 kg/m³, steel 7880 kg/m³.

analysis: The aluminium cube has a density of 72.9 ÷ 27.0 = 2.70 g/cm³ (2700 kg/m³), which matches the accepted value for aluminium. The steel cuboid has a density of 236.4 ÷ 30.0 = 7.88 g/cm³, close to the accepted value of about 7.9 g/cm³.
The stone has a density of 47.7 ÷ 18.0 = 2.65 g/cm³, which is typical of rocks such as granite or sandstone. Its volume could only be found by displacement because its shape is irregular.
Water has a density of about 1.00 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³). Cooking oil has a lower density (0.92 g/cm³), which is why oil floats on water.

Metals have the highest densities because their atoms are heavy and closely packed. Density depends on the material, not on the size of the sample: a larger aluminium block would have a larger mass and volume, but the same density.
The eureka can method gives the least precise result, because some water stays on the spout and inside the measuring cylinder, and the 100 cm³ cylinder has a resolution of only 1 cm³.

errors.error: Water clinging to the spout of the eureka can or drops still falling, so less water is collected and the volume is too small (density too large).
errors.improvement: Wait until dripping has completely stopped both before and after adding the object, and tap the spout gently.

errors.error: Parallax error when reading the measuring cylinder, or reading the top of the meniscus.
errors.improvement: Read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus, with the cylinder on a flat surface.

errors.error: A measuring cylinder with a large scale (100 cm³) has poor resolution for small volumes.
errors.improvement: Use the smallest measuring cylinder that will hold the displaced water, such as a 10 cm³ or 25 cm³ cylinder.

errors.error: Small objects measured with a ruler have a large percentage uncertainty in each dimension.
errors.improvement: Use vernier callipers or a micrometer, and measure each dimension in several places to calculate a mean.

errors.error: Splashing water out of the can by dropping the object in, giving too large a volume.
errors.improvement: Lower the object gently on a thread.

examTips: Learn density = mass ÷ volume (ρ = m ÷ V) and be able to rearrange it to find mass or volume.
Convert carefully: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
For an irregular object, describe the eureka can fully: fill to the spout, wait for dripping to stop, lower the object on a thread, collect and measure the displaced water.
Always say 'read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus' when using a measuring cylinder.
When asked for an improvement, choose equipment with a better resolution: vernier callipers instead of a ruler, or a smaller measuring cylinder.

questions.question: Which equation is used to calculate density?
questions.explanation: Density is the mass per unit volume, so it is mass divided by volume (ρ = m ÷ V). Students must recall this equation.

questions.question:
A metal cube has sides of 3.0 cm and a mass of 72.9 g.
Calculate the density of the metal in g/cm³.
questions.explanation: Find the volume of the cube first (side cubed), then divide the mass by the volume. Using 3.0 cm as the volume gives 24.3 g/cm³, which is wrong.

questions.question:
The density of aluminium is 2.7 g/cm³.
What is the density of aluminium in kg/m³?
questions.explanation: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so multiply by 1000. There are 1000 g in 1 kg and 1 000 000 cm³ in 1 m³.

questions.question:
A stone with a mass of 47.7 g is lowered into a full eureka can. 18.0 cm³ of water is collected in a measuring cylinder.
Calculate the density of the stone.
markScheme: 1 mark: volume of stone = 18.0 cm³ (volume of water displaced)
questions.explanation: The stone displaces its own volume of water, so its volume is 18.0 cm³. Density = 47.7 ÷ 18.0 = 2.65 g/cm³.

questions.question: A student fills a eureka can with water until it overflows. Explain why the student must wait until the water stops dripping from the spout before putting the object into the can.
acceptedAnswers: so only the displaced water is collected
markScheme: 1 mark: so the water level is exactly at the spout / the can is just full
1 mark: otherwise extra water (not displaced by the object) would be collected, making the measured volume too large
questions.explanation: Only the water pushed out by the object should go into the measuring cylinder. Extra drips would make the volume too large and the calculated density too small.

questions.question: Which apparatus is best for measuring the volume of an irregularly shaped stone?
options: A eureka can and a measuring cylinder
markScheme: 1 mark: a eureka can and a measuring cylinder
questions.explanation: An irregular object cannot be measured with a ruler or callipers. Its volume is found by displacement: the volume of water it pushes out of a eureka can equals its own volume.

questions.question:
A steel cuboid measures 2.0 cm × 3.0 cm × 5.0 cm and has a mass of 236.4 g.
Calculate the density of the steel. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height = 30 cm³. 236.4 ÷ 30 = 7.88 g/cm³.

questions.question:
An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 62.5 g. When 50.0 cm³ of cooking oil is added, the total mass is 108.3 g.
Calculate the density of the oil. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Subtract the mass of the empty cylinder to find the mass of oil alone. 45.8 ÷ 50.0 = 0.916 g/cm³, which is 0.92 g/cm³ to 2 significant figures. Using 108.3 g gives 2.17 g/cm³, which is wrong.

questions.question: Describe how a student should read the volume of water in a measuring cylinder accurately.
markScheme: 1 mark: with eye level with the water surface (to avoid parallax)
1 mark: read from the bottom of the meniscus
questions.explanation: Reading from above or below eye level gives a parallax error. The water surface curves, so the reading is taken from the bottom of the curve (meniscus).

questions.question:
A block of aluminium has a volume of 0.00040 m³. The density of aluminium is 2700 kg/m³.
Calculate the mass of the block.
questions.explanation: Rearrange ρ = m ÷ V to m = ρ × V. 2700 × 0.00040 = 1.08 kg.

questions.question:
An object has a mass of 0.540 kg and a volume of 0.000200 m³.
Calculate its density in kg/m³.
questions.explanation: Mass in kg and volume in m³ give density in kg/m³. 0.540 ÷ 0.000200 = 2700 kg/m³. Errors with powers of ten are common, so check the answer is sensible for a solid.

questions.question: When using a eureka can, some displaced water stays on the spout and is not collected. What effect does this have on the calculated density of the object?
options: The density is too small, because the volume measured is too large
The density is too large, because the volume measured is too small
The density is too large, because the mass measured is too large
There is no effect, because the mass is measured separately
markScheme: 1 mark: density too large because the measured volume is too small
questions.explanation: Less water is collected than the object really displaced, so the measured volume is too small. Dividing the correct mass by a smaller volume gives a larger density.

questions.question:
A student measures the sides of a small metal cube, about 1 cm across, with a ruler marked in millimetres.
Suggest a better instrument to use and explain why it is better.
markScheme: 1 mark: higher resolution (for example 0.1 mm or 0.01 mm), so a smaller percentage uncertainty in the volume
questions.explanation: A 1 mm uncertainty in 10 mm is 10%, and cubing the length makes the error in volume even bigger. Callipers read to 0.1 mm or better.

questions.question: Explain why cooking oil, with a density of 0.92 g/cm³, floats on water, with a density of 1.00 g/cm³.
acceptedAnswers: oil is less dense than water
markScheme: 1 mark: oil has a lower density than water
questions.explanation: A liquid with a lower density floats on top of a liquid with a higher density. Equal volumes of oil have less mass than water.

questions.question:
Describe a method to determine the density of an irregularly shaped stone.
Include the equipment used and how the density is calculated.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure the mass of the stone with a top pan balance (zeroed first); fill a eureka can with water until it overflows from the spout; wait until dripping stops; place an empty measuring cylinder under the spout; tie the stone to a thread and lower it gently into the water until fully submerged; collect the displaced water; read the volume at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus; volume of water = volume of stone; density = mass ÷ volume; give units (g/cm³ or kg/m³); repeat and find a mean; alternative: lower the stone into a measuring cylinder part filled with water and find the rise in water level

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent method that measures both mass and volume correctly by displacement, with detail such as filling to the spout, waiting for dripping to stop and reading the meniscus, and the density calculation stated.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method that measures mass and volume by displacement, with some detail missing, or the calculation not fully stated.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as weigh the stone and put it in water, without a clear way to find the volume.
questions.explanation: Top answers explain why the water must be level with the spout before starting, how the object is lowered without splashing, how the volume is read accurately, and use density = mass ÷ volume.
